title: The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Cortex
subtitle: Lobar landmarks, aphasias, agnosias, neglect, apraxias and frontal syndromes: what each cortical region tells you

points.text: On the lateral surface the Sylvian fissure and the Rolandic (central) sulcus separate the temporal, frontal and parietal lobes; the occipital lobe is the most posterior part.
points.quote: the frontal lobe, anterior to the Rolandic or central sulcus; and the parietal lobe, posterior to the Rolandic sulcus

points.text: The precentral gyrus holds the primary motor area.
points.quote: The precentral gyrus contains the primary motor area

points.text: Heschl transverse gyrus is the primary auditory area and forms the anterior limit of the planum temporale.
points.quote: It is the primary auditory area and the anterior limit of the planum temporale or supratemporal plane

points.text: The lowest part of the postcentral gyrus, next to the Sylvian fissure, is the secondary somatosensory cortex.
points.quote: The most inferior extent of this gyrus, abutting the Sylvian fissure, contains the secondary somatosensory cortex.

points.text: The inferior parietal lobule wraps around the end of the Sylvian sulcus anteriorly as the supramarginal gyrus (and posteriorly around the superior temporal sulcus as the angular gyrus).
points.quote: Anteriorly, the inferior parietal lobule curves around the posterior extent of the Sylvian sulcus (supramarginal gyrus)

coreAnatomy.title: Primary, secondary and multimodal association cortex

points.text: Primary areas receive sensory input or project to motor nuclei; the rest of the cortex is association cortex, which mainly makes corticocortical connections.
points.quote: contrast with the rest of the cortex, named association cortex, giving rise preferentially to corticocortical connections

points.text: Cortex next to a primary sensory area handles one modality (unimodal).
points.quote: the cortex adjacent to the primary sensory areas (secondary sensory areas) processes unimodal sensory information, often keeping a somatotopic organization

points.text: Cortex between the secondary areas is tertiary and combines modalities.
points.quote: whereas the cortex lying between the different secondary sensory areas (tertiary sensory cortex) integrates multimodal sensory information

points.text: Somatosensory information joins auditory and visual information in the angular gyrus.
points.quote: Somatotopic information is integrated with auditory and visual information in the inferoposterior portions of the inferior parietal lobule (angular gyrus)

points.text: A primary lesion causes loss of the modality, whereas a multimodal association lesion produces deficits of integrated performance.
points.quote: Lesions of the primary somatosensory area result in sensory loss, whereas lesions in the multimodal association areas result in motor performances

points.text: The right hemisphere is dominant for spatial and constructional skills, directed attention and body image.
points.quote: the right hemisphere is dominant for tasks requiring spatial and constructional skills, as well as for directed attention and body image

points.text: The left hemisphere is dominant for language, motor functions and linguistic reasoning.
points.quote: whereas the left hemisphere is dominant for language and motor functions, as well as linguistic thought and reasoning

points.text: Wernicke area (area 22) is the posterior superior temporal auditory association cortex; its infarction gives the greatest impairment of auditory comprehension.
points.quote: Ischemia or infarction centered in the posterior two-thirds of the superior temporal gyrus affecting the auditory association cortex

points.text: Broca area is the inferior left frontal gyrus (areas 44 and 45); true Broca aphasia needs more extensive damage around it.
points.quote: extensive damage involving not only Broca area (the inferior left frontal gyrus, which contains areas 44 and 45)

points.text: Active, goal-directed attention uses a dorsal system and involves both hemispheres.
points.quote: Active attention is mediated by a dorsal system including the superior parietal lobule and the superior portion of the dorsal prefrontal cortex

points.text: Because the right hemisphere alerts for both sides of the body, attentional impairment is more frequent and more pervasive with right-sided lesions.
points.quote: As the right hemisphere provides alerting mechanisms for both sides of the body, attentional impairment occurs more often and is more pervasive

points.text: A unilateral mesencephalic reticular lesion can produce contralateral inattention through hypoarousal of the hemisphere.
points.quote: unilateral lesions of the mesencephalic reticular formation result in contralateral inattention, probably because of unilateral hypoarousal of the hemisphere

coreAnatomy.title: Frontal motor organization and memory circuits

points.text: Large bilateral mesial frontal (cingulate, supplementary motor) lesions leave an alert-looking patient motionless and mute.
points.quote: Although seemingly alert, patients with large bilateral lesions in this region remain motionless and mute (akinetic mutism)

points.text: The primary motor cortex is more important for fine distal movements; axial movements such as walking depend more on subcortical structures.
points.quote: The primary motor cortex plays a greater role in the execution of fine, distal movements

points.text: The amnestic syndrome arises from damage to medial temporal structures, anteromedial thalamic nuclei or their connections.
points.quote: damage the medial temporal lobes, especially the amygdala and hippocampus; the anterior and dorsomedial nuclei of the thalamus; or the connections of these structures

points.text: Bilateral lesions of Papez circuit structures have been reported to cause amnesia.
points.quote: lesions, usually bilateral, of any of the structures of Papez circuit (hippocampus, fornix, mammillary body, mammillothalamic tract,

localizationRules.explanation: Seizures plus multimodal deficits (aphasia, apraxia) point to cortex; weakness, spasticity, field deficits, pure motor syndromes and urinary incontinence point to white matter.
localizationRules.quote: Characteristic of cortical lesions are (1) seizures and (2) multimodal motor and sensory deficits, such as aphasia and apraxia.

localizationRules.rule: Tempo and nature of the lesion
localizationRules.explanation: A sudden destructive lesion gives a more severe deficit than a slowly infiltrating tumor in the same place, so localization of diffuse lesions is less accurate.
localizationRules.quote: small infarcts often cause aphasia, but tumors have to be quite large before they cause an aphasic syndrome

localizationRules.rule: Do not pinpoint a square centimeter
localizationRules.explanation: Cortical functions are subserved by networks and vary between individuals, so name the likely region, not the exact spot.
localizationRules.quote: any attempt to pinpoint the exact square centimeter of the cortex that accounts for a deficit in a particular patient is a futile endeavor

localizationRules.rule: Temporal lesion gives sensory aphasia, frontal gives motor aphasia
localizationRules.explanation: Posterior (temporal) lesions impair comprehension of the spoken word; frontal lesions give sparse agrammatical language with comprehension spared.
localizationRules.quote: patients with predominantly temporal lesions had a sensory or receptive aphasia, interfering with the comprehension of the spoken word

localizationRules.explanation: Global aphasia with hemiplegia means damage to the anterior language area, the basal ganglia region, the insula and the posterior language region, usually a large MCA infarct.
localizationRules.quote: The presence or absence of hemiplegia is an important clue to the localization of brain damage

localizationRules.rule: Neglect points to the right inferior parietal lobule
localizationRules.explanation: Neglect appears more readily and profoundly with right-hemisphere lesions; the right inferior parietal lobule is the classic site.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions of the right inferior parietal lobule are especially apt to cause this syndrome.

localizationRules.rule: Primary cortex versus unimodal association cortex
localizationRules.explanation: A primary lesion causes loss of that modality; an association-cortex lesion causes extinction on double simultaneous stimulation (visual areas 18 and 19; anterior parietal for touch).
localizationRules.quote: Whereas unilateral lesions of primary cortex cause contralateral unimodal sensory loss, lesions of unimodal association cortex impair the perception of contralateral versus ipsilateral stimuli

keySyndromes.name: Wernicke aphasia
keySyndromes.triad: Fluent speech + impaired repetition + impaired naming + paraphasic errors (impaired comprehension)
keySyndromes.clue: Posterior superior temporal lesion, most commonly from an inferior division MCA infarct; hemiparesis and sensory loss may be absent or mild, so it can be misdiagnosed as psychiatric.
keySyndromes.quote: Patients with Wernicke aphasia are unable to repeat sentences correctly, to assemble phonemes correctly, and to name things properly, but their speech is fluent

keySyndromes.name: Broca aphasia
keySyndromes.triad: Drastic loss of fluency + agrammatic telegraphic speech + impaired repetition + impaired naming helped by cueing
keySyndromes.clue: Lasting Broca aphasia corresponds to lesions extending across the frontoparietal operculum, not to Broca area alone.
keySyndromes.quote: There is a drastic loss of speech fluency, with speech becoming effortful and often slow, with pauses between words often outnumbering the words themselves

keySyndromes.name: Conduction aphasia
keySyndromes.triad: Intelligible speech + good enough comprehension + impaired repetition + paraphasic errors
keySyndromes.clue: Circumscribed lesions of the supramarginal gyrus (area 40) or auditory cortex; the book notes the traditional arcuate fasciculus explanation is not well supported.
keySyndromes.quote: Patients with conduction aphasia speak intelligibly and comprehend well enough to maintain a normal conversation, but their ability to repeat is impaired

keySyndromes.name: Transcortical sensory aphasia
keySyndromes.triad: Good repetition + impaired comprehension of spoken and written words + echolalia
keySyndromes.clue: Analogue of Wernicke aphasia with spared repetition; posterior left middle temporal and angular gyrus region, with little localizing value, often MCA/PCA watershed ischemia.
keySyndromes.quote: Some patients can repeat words well but are unable to understand the meaning of the spoken or written word

keySyndromes.name: Transcortical motor aphasia
keySyndromes.triad: Lack of verbal spontaneity + correct repetition + telegraphic speech or perseveration
keySyndromes.clue: Dominant frontal lesion anterior or superior to Broca area, or supplementary motor area; ACA infarct or ACA-MCA border zone.
keySyndromes.quote: transcortical motor aphasia differs from Broca in that the patient can repeat correctly and may even correct syntactic errors in the original sentence

keySyndromes.name: Alexia without agraphia (pure word blindness)
keySyndromes.triad: Cannot read + writes on dictation + usually right homonymous hemianopia or hemiachromatopsia + often color agnosia
keySyndromes.clue: Dominant medial occipital lesion plus the inferior splenium disconnects visual input from the intact dominant angular gyrus; alexia with agraphia is the angular gyrus syndrome instead.
keySyndromes.quote: Patients cannot read but are able to write on dictation.

keySyndromes.name: Balint syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Failure to shift gaze (apraxia of gaze) + optic ataxia + decreased visual attention with tunnel vision
keySyndromes.clue: Bilateral parietooccipital convexity lesions (watershed) and often visual simultanagnosia.
keySyndromes.quote: the Balint syndrome, which follows bilateral parietooccipital lesions in the convexity of the hemispheres

keySyndromes.name: Gerstmann syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Finger agnosia + right-left disorientation + agraphia + acalculia
keySyndromes.clue: Dominant angular and supramarginal gyri; the book cites necropsy cases with all four signs and an intact angular gyrus.
keySyndromes.quote: Gerstmann described the association of these four signs (Gerstmann syndrome) as characteristic of lesions in the angular and supramarginal gyri

boardTraps.text: A lesion restricted to Broca area or its subjacent white matter does not produce true, lasting Broca aphasia, only a mild transient aphasia.
boardTraps.quote: When damage is restricted to Brocas area alone or to its subjacent white matter, true Broca aphasia does not develop

boardTraps.text: Acute global aphasia after a large perisylvian stroke often evolves into Broca aphasia as comprehension improves, so the label depends on timing.
boardTraps.quote: Acutely after stroke, patients that will eventually develop classical Broca aphasia often have global aphasia.

boardTraps.text: Global aphasia without hemiparesis is possible: it may be a single dominant temporoparietal lesion, but more often two discrete dominant-hemisphere lesions, one frontal and one temporoparietal (usually embolic).
boardTraps.quote: Global aphasia without other lateralizing signs (i.e., no hemiparesis or lasting motor defects) may occur with a single dominant temporoparietal lesion

boardTraps.text: Visual inattention can masquerade as hemianopia; a patient may detect a left-field stimulus when the eyes are turned to the right, so the hemispace of presentation matters.
boardTraps.quote: This patient had hemispatial visual inattention masquerading as hemianopia.

boardTraps.text: Anosognosia is often seen with right-hemisphere lesions but does not require neglect.
boardTraps.quote: However, it need not be associated with a neglect syndrome, and often it is not

boardTraps.text: Anton syndrome: a patient who is blind from bilateral extensive medial occipital lesions denies the blindness and confabulates; discrete lesions usually extend to areas 18 and 19.
boardTraps.quote: Patients with acute, bilateral, and extensive medial occipital lesions that render them blind may deny having any difficulty with seeing (visual anosognosia) and confabulate

boardTraps.text: Subcortical aphasia is debated: the book calls it controversial whether pure subcortical lesions can cause true aphasia, and notes that MCA stem occlusion also ischemias the posterior perisylvian cortex.
boardTraps.quote: It is controversial whether pure subcortical lesions can cause true aphasia
